There was something strange in all this that fascinated and enchanted me. It was as though he had finally awakened from a long, dream-filled sleep. He felt rather like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad in that lovely imitation of an Eastern tale. Diana was gone; his friends had changed or died; and upon waking, he found that I was all he had left to love on earth.

How precious the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became, now that someone I loved so deeply shared my walks. With my father I visited every delightful place: the islands, the waterfalls sheltered by trees, each shaded path and every hollow tangled with ferns and undergrowth. Talking with him broadened my mind. I felt remade, filled with the freshness and vitality of a new being. Since his arrival, I seemed to have been carried from a tiny patch of earth into a universe without limits for either imagination or understanding. Before, my life had resembled a pleasant country stream, destined never to leave its native fields but quietly to sink into the earth when its work was done, leaving no trace. Now it seemed a river flowing through a fertile, lovely landscape, constantly changing and constantly beautiful. Alas, I knew nothing of the desert it was approaching, the rocks that would tear its waters, or the dreadful scene its waves would reflect in still more distorted forms. Life was radiant then. I began to learn hope, and what brings the heart more bitter despair than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should follow such heavenly happiness so swiftly? I drank from an enchanted cup, but beneath its lingering sweetness lay bitterness. My heart overflowed with profound affection, and the very depth and fullness of that feeling made it calm. I had never imagined that love could produce misery. That lesson, which everyone eventually learns, came to me in a form few are forced to endure. I mourn now, and always must mourn, those brief months of paradise. I broke no commandment, ate no apple, yet I was mercilessly driven out. Alas, my companion did, and his fall dragged me down with him. But I am straying from my story. Let sorrow arrive at its appointed hour; at this point I may still speak of happiness.

Three months of this delightful companionship passed before my aunt became ill. I spent a whole month nursing her in her room, but the illness was fatal. She died, leaving me inconsolable for a time. Death is so terrible to those still living. Habit binds us so strongly, even without affection to join its links, that breaking those bonds must torment the heart.

The next day the ghost felt very weak and tired. The terrible strain of the previous four weeks was taking its toll. His nerves were shattered, and the slightest noise made him jump. He stayed in his room for five days and finally decided to give up maintaining the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family did not want it, they plainly did not deserve it. They were evidently people who cared only about ordinary material things and could not appreciate the symbolic meaning of what their senses showed them. Appearing as a ghost and taking on a visible spirit body were, of course, different matters, and not really his choice. He had a solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week and make terrifying noises from the large projecting window on the first and third Wednesday of every month. He could see no honourable way to avoid these obligations. His life had admittedly been very wicked, but he took every supernatural responsibility seriously. For the next three Saturdays, then, he walked the corridor as usual between midnight and three in the morning, taking every precaution against being seen or heard. He removed his boots, stepped as softly as possible on the old worm-eaten floorboards, wore a large black velvet cloak, and carefully oiled his chains with the Rising Sun Lubricator. I must admit that persuading himself to adopt this last precaution was very difficult. Nevertheless, one evening while the family ate dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis's bedroom and took the bottle. At first he felt rather humiliated. Later, he sensibly recognized the invention's advantages, and it helped him to some extent. Even so, he was not left in peace. Strings kept appearing across the corridor, tripping him in the dark. Once, while dressed as 'Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,' he suffered a serious fall after stepping onto a slippery trail of butter. The twins had spread it from the Tapestry Chamber's entrance to the top of the oak staircase. This final insult enraged him so much that he decided on one last attempt to defend his dignity and social standing. The next night he would visit the rude young Eton boys in his famous role of 'Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.'

He had not used this disguise in more than seventy years. The last occasion had frightened pretty Lady Barbara Modish so badly that she abruptly broke her engagement to the present Lord Canterville's grandfather and ran away to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton. She declared that nothing could persuade her to marry into a family that allowed such a dreadful ghost to wander the terrace at dusk.

My father's surname was Pirrip and my first name was Philip, but as a small child I could turn those names into nothing longer or clearer than Pip. So I called myself Pip, and everyone else did too.

I know my father's surname from his gravestone and from my sister, Mrs. Joe Gargery, who married the blacksmith. I never saw either parent, nor any picture of them; they lived long before photographs existed. My earliest ideas of their appearance came, rather foolishly, from their gravestones. The shape of the lettering on my father's gave me the strange impression that he had been a broad, stout, dark man with curly black hair. From the style of the words 'Also Georgiana, Wife of the Above,' I concluded that my mother had freckles and poor health. Beside their grave stood a tidy row of five small, diamond-shaped stones, each about a foot and a half long. They commemorated my five little brothers, who had abandoned the universal struggle to make a living exceptionally early. Those stones gave me a belief I held with absolute conviction: all five had been born lying on their backs, hands in their trouser pockets, and had never taken them out during their lives.

We lived in marsh country beside the river, within twenty miles of the sea if you followed its bends. My first vivid, complete sense of what everything around me meant came, I think, on one unforgettable chilly afternoon as evening approached. I understood for certain that the bleak, nettle-covered place was the churchyard. Philip Pirrip, once of this parish, and Georgiana, his wife, were dead and buried there. So were their infant sons Alexander, Bartholomew, Abraham, Tobias, and Roger. The dark, flat wilderness stretching beyond the churchyard, divided by ditches, banks, and gates, with scattered cattle grazing across it, was the marshes. The low, lead-grey line beyond was the river. Farther still lay the savage home of the wind rushing toward me: the sea. And the little bundle of shivers, frightened by all of it and beginning to cry, was Pip.

'Stop that noise!' roared a dreadful voice. A man sprang up among the graves beside the church porch. 'Keep quiet, you little devil, or I'll cut your throat!'

He was a terrifying man, dressed entirely in rough grey cloth, with a heavy iron shackle on his leg.
